vignette:
# The Weight of the Chainsaw

Marcus is a 54-year-old forester who has spent the better part of three decades working the timber stands of the Pacific Northwest. He knows the forest the way most people know their own living rooms — the sound of a widow-maker shifting in the wind, the way a tree telegraphs its fall before it moves. He has always prided himself on that knowledge. It is, in large part, who he is.

Two years ago, on an unremarkable Tuesday morning in late October, Marcus was supervising a routine selective harvest on a steep hillside. His crew was experienced. The plan was sound. He had done the same job hundreds of times. He gave the signal, and a large Douglas fir came down — but not the way it was supposed to. The tree kicked back off a hidden stump, pivoting sharply, and struck Danny, a 28-year-old who had been working with Marcus for three seasons. The impact shattered Danny's pelvis and left femur. Danny spent four months in the hospital. He walks now, but with a permanent limp, and he has not returned to forestry work.

Marcus rode in the helicopter with Danny that day. He held his hand and watched the color drain from the young man's face. By the time they landed, Marcus had already begun the process of deciding it was entirely his fault.

The investigation that followed cleared Marcus of any negligence. The stump had been buried under debris and was not visible during the site assessment. His supervisor told him it was an accident. His wife, Colleen, told him the same. Marcus heard all of it and believed none of it.

He returned to work six weeks later because he did not know what else to do. But the forest he came back to was not the same one he had left. Now, when he walks a stand, he finds himself frozen at moments that once felt automatic — hesitating before giving a felling signal, rechecking angles he has already checked twice, running scenarios of what could go wrong until the mental noise becomes almost unbearable. Some mornings he sits in his truck at the job site for twenty minutes before he can open the door.

At night, sleep comes in fragments. He wakes at two or three in the morning with the sound of Danny's voice in his head — not screaming, which might be easier to dismiss, but the quiet, confused way Danny said *Marcus* right after it happened, as though he was trying to make sense of something. Marcus lies in the dark beside Colleen and does not wake her. He has become skilled at keeping his distress contained, which mostly means keeping it invisible.

He has grown quieter at home. Colleen has noticed. Their adult son visited last Thanksgiving and mentioned to Colleen afterward that his father seemed "somewhere else." Marcus is aware of the distance he is creating but finds it difficult to bridge. Conversation requires a kind of presence he struggles to sustain. He still goes through the motions — dinner, weekend chores, the occasional walk with Colleen — but there is a flatness to it that he cannot seem to lift.

He visited Danny once, about eight months after the accident. Danny was gracious. He said he didn't blame Marcus. The visit made everything worse. Marcus drove home and sat in the driveway for an hour, unable to go inside.

What troubles Marcus most, perhaps, is that he no longer trusts himself in the place that has always defined him. The forest used to be where he felt most competent, most alive. Now it is where he feels most dangerous. He still goes, because not going feels like surrender, and because he doesn't know who he is without the work. But he goes carrying something heavy that has no name he is willing to give it yet.
